pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your database leaks. Why is a salted SHA-256 of each password still a bad night, and what does bcrypt (or Argon2id) change?
expected_points: general-purpose hashes are built to be fast — GPUs do billions of guesses per second, so common passwords fall immediately
a password KDF has a tunable work factor that makes each guess expensive, and Argon2id also makes it memory-expensive
the salt is public and per-password: it defeats precomputed tables and hides shared passwords, it does not slow anything down
cost is raised over time; a successful login is the moment to re-hash at the new cost

questions.prompt: Walk me through the session cookie your service sets. What does each attribute stop, and what does the server still have to do itself?
expected_points: HttpOnly keeps JavaScript (and therefore XSS) away from the id
Secure keeps it off plain HTTP; SameSite=Lax keeps it off cross-site requests, blunting CSRF
Max-Age is only advice to the browser — the server enforces expiry on every lookup against its own clock
the id must come from crypto/rand, not math/rand/v2, and means nothing on its own: the server holds the state

questions.prompt: Why does login mint a brand new session id even when the request already carried one, and why does promoting a user to admin do it again?
expected_points: session fixation: an id the attacker planted must never become an authenticated id
an id captured before a privilege change must not be usable after it
rotation destroys the old id server-side, so the old cookie stops working immediately
logout is the same idea taken further: the server deletes the session, not just the cookie

questions.prompt: I hand your service a JWT. In what order do you check things, and what goes wrong if you read the claims first?
expected_points: split, pin alg to exactly HS256, verify the signature, only then parse and trust claims, then check exp
alg is attacker-controlled input: alg=none and algorithm confusion (RS256 expected, HS256 supplied, public key used as the HMAC secret)
the signature is compared with hmac.Equal / crypto/subtle, never ==, so it leaks no timing
a token with no exp never expires; expiry must be checked against an injected clock

questions.prompt: Sessions or JWTs: what does each side actually store, and which would you pick for a first-party web app? For calls between your own services?
expected_points: sessions keep state server-side and hand out an opaque id; a JWT carries signed state the client holds
sessions are revocable by deletion; a JWT is valid until it expires unless you rebuild state (denylist, token version, refresh tokens)
sessions need a shared store to scale out; token verification needs no lookup
first-party browser app → session; service-to-service or several verifiers → tokens, with short lifetimes

questions.prompt: Sketch the authorization-code-with-PKCE flow, and tell me where OIDC differs from plain OAuth2.
expected_points: redirect to the provider with state and a code_challenge (hash of a code_verifier you keep); the user authenticates there, never against your service
the provider redirects back with a code; you compare state, then your server exchanges the code plus code_verifier for tokens
PKCE proves the party redeeming the code is the one that started the flow, so an intercepted code is useless
OAuth2 delegates authorization; OIDC adds an id_token (a JWT about the user) validated against the provider's JWKS — and you still issue your own session
use a library (x/oauth2, go-oidc): discovery, key rotation, nonce and skew handling are where hand-rolled versions break

questions.prompt: Why does the login handler verify a password against a dummy hash when the username does not exist — and how does the test prove it without measuring time?
expected_points: otherwise response time (and message) reveal whether an account exists: user enumeration
identical status, identical body, and identical work on both paths
the test counts Verify calls through a wrapping hasher; timing assertions would be flaky under -race

questions.prompt: A user's laptop is stolen with a live token that expires in 12 hours. What are your options, and what do they cost?
expected_points: nothing consults the server when a signed token is used, so it stays valid until exp
options: very short access tokens plus a server-side refresh token, a jti denylist, or a per-user token version
each option restores a server lookup — the statelessness that motivated JWTs is partly given back
with a session it is one delete
